A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Bayesian account of in-context learning and activation steering. The text, equations, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial layout changes and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments on three LLMs across five persona datasets, including held-out Bayesian predictions, steering responses, phase boundaries, and supplementary analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds experiments with Llama-3.1-70B, higher-prior persona traits, and flipped-label sentiment analysis.

M1.justification: CAA steering, the four-parameter Bayesian log-odds model, and its fitting procedure remain unchanged (v1 Eq. 8; v2 Eq. 9). The sentiment experiment applies the same difference-in-means construction to standard versus rotated labels; it introduces no new algorithmic component.

E1.justification: Beyond the five retained persona datasets, v2 adds three-label Financial PhraseBank sentiment analysis with rotated labels and higher-prior traits. Figure 16 shows Openness, Interest in Science, Interest in Music, and Desire to Create Allies. Section 3 inconsistently lists Machiavellianism instead of Openness, but the substantial expansion beyond the original coverage is clear.

E2.justification: Neither version evaluates additional competing prediction models or steering algorithms. The Bayesian-versus-observed-behavior comparisons and CAA controls are retained. Llama-3.1-70B is an additional system whose behavior is modeled.

E3.justification: The added evaluations substantially expand model scale and context length: Appendix D tests Llama-3.1-70B, and Figure 17 evaluates sentiment learning with up to 320 shots, beyond v1's 7–9B models and persona contexts of up to 128 shots. The original experiments retain their sampling, fitting, and ten-fold cross-validation settings.

E4.justification: Appendix E adds a targeted test of whether the predicted steering dynamics persist for concepts with high initial prior probability, extending v1's low-prior focus. The existing extreme-magnitude breakdown, layer-sensitivity, and many-shot steering-vector analyses are retained.

E5.justification: v2 first reports p < .001 for correlations in Section 3 and for the crossover correlation in Figure 8; v1 reported the correlations without these significance statements. No increase in repeated runs or change to uncertainty-estimation procedures is documented.

E6.justification: The original headline correlations remain unchanged, but Appendices D–F add held-out prediction correlations of 0.98 for Llama-3.1-70B, 0.87 for higher-prior traits, and 0.96 for flipped-label sentiment. New findings include faster persona acquisition in the 70B model and substantially more shots needed for sentiment-label rotation. These are additional results under new conditions, not improvements on the original measurements.

T1.justification: v2 adds Appendix A.2 deriving the existing posterior approximation; the original Bayes-factor and steering-magnitude derivations are retained. The added algebra contains an inconsistent transition from a positive beta_i*a term to a negative one. The underlying assumptions and final model remain unchanged.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and concluding discussion retain the same central contributions: a unified Bayesian account, steering as prior modification, context as evidence accumulation, and additive effects that predict behavioral phase boundaries. The new experiments support these existing claims.

C2.justification: Section 4.1 adds a qualification about sharper increases or earlier plateaus for high-prior concepts. Appendices E–F interpret the new results as supporting applicability to high-prior traits and non-binary response labels. The existing mechanistic discussion and limitations concerning binary latent concepts, CAA, and excessive steering remain.

D1.justification: Figure 17 documents the cyclic label permutation and construction of steering vectors from standard versus rotated labels, while Appendix H identifies the added 70B Instruct checkpoint. v1's direct persona-dataset repository link is removed. The steering-code link, quantization, hardware, and original optimizer details are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds Malo et al. (2014) for the financial sentiment dataset, listed twice as 2014a and 2014b, and connects the new task to the already-cited Agarwal et al. work. Its broader positioning relative to Bayesian ICL and linear representation research is unchanged.

P1.justification: v2 lightly edits the abstract and other passages, updates headings and affiliation text, and expands Section 3 and the appendices to accommodate the additions. The main section order, explanatory narrative, and most discussion prose are retained.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from one-column to two-column formatting, Figure 3 rearranges its schematic panels, and new Figures 7 and 15–17 display the added experiments. Numerous retained figures are relocated and rescaled, including a substantial reduction in the displayed size of Figure 5.

improvement.justification: The new 70B, high-prior, and three-label sentiment experiments provide broader held-out support for the unchanged account than v1's small-model persona evaluations. This is a limited net gain: settings for the new experiments remain sparsely documented, Section 3 conflicts with Figure 16 about one trait, and the added Appendix A.2 introduces sign-inconsistent algebra. The empirical support improves more clearly than the theoretical rigor or reproducibility.
